title: World Cup games face significant risk of ‘serious heat illness’ says international research group
content:
Fans and players at this summer’s World Cup in North America face a significant risk of “serious heat illness” because of high temperatures and humidity, according to a new study by international research group World Weather Attribution (WWA).

After six games at last summer’s Club World Cup were disrupted by heat and storms, FIFA has responded to criticism of its extreme-weather policies by introducing mandatory, three-minute “cooling breaks” for this tournament, which starts in Mexico City on June 11.

But in a 52-page report published on Thursday, World Weather Attribution’s scientists claim that approximately 26 of the 104 games are likely to be played when the host city’s Wet Bulb Global Temperature (WBGT) exceeds 26 degrees, with five games at the six-week tournament likely to be played in conditions with an WBGT that exceeds 28 degrees.

A measure of heat stress, WBGT combines temperature, humidity, wind and sunlight, and it is used by the military, sports scientists and safety experts to prevent heat-related illnesses.

“Heat risk should not be judged by air temperature alone,” said WWA’s Dr Chris Mullington, a senior lecturer at Imperial College London.

“A 30-degree day in dry, breezy conditions is very different from a 30-degree day with high humidity, strong sun and little wind. High humidity reduces the evaporation of sweat, limiting the body’s primary cooling mechanism – that is why WBGT is important.

“When it exceeds 26 degrees, player performance can suffer. Above 28 degrees, the risk of serious heat illness becomes more concerning – not only for players, but also for hundreds of thousands of fans in stadiums and outdoor fan festivals.

“Heat stroke, the most severe form of heat illness, is life-threatening and older people with pre-existing medical conditions are particularly vulnerable.”

Before to this summer, FIFA had only allowed referees to halt play for a water break if the WBGT hit 32 degrees, a threshold considerably higher than the safety thresholds used by other sports, such as athletics and cycling.

Calls for FIFA to lower its threshold, most notably from global players’ union FIFPro, appear to have been at least partly heeded, as world football’s governing body has effectively split the games into four quarters this summer. But it has not revealed its threshold for postponing a game, which FIFPro believes should happen when the WBGT exceeds 28 degrees.

“My understanding is that the 32-degree limit is somewhat of a historical threshold,” said Mullington.

“Other sports used to align with that level and have become more conservative in their recommendations over the years. FIFA don’t seem to have moved on from that threshold, possibly because they haven’t had a seminal medical event for a player which has forced their hand. But I do agree that they lag behind other world sporting bodies.”

FIFPro welcomed the introduction of mandatory cooling breaks when they were announced in December, and also praised FIFA for thinking about potential heat-stress risks when it scheduled matches for this summer’s tournament, but told The Athletic there has been no discussion about the WBGT threshold FIFA considers to be unsafe for play.

In a media briefing to launch the report, WWA’s Dr Friederike Otto, a professor of climate science at Imperial College London, described conditions of 28 degrees WBGT as “positively dangerous and not just for players but also for fans”.

The venues most likely to stage games under those conditions are in Atlanta, Dallas and Houston, although all three of those stadiums have roofs and air-conditioning, which will greatly mitigate the players’ risks.

The report, however, points out that fans, both at the games and in fan festivals, will have to take precautions to avoid heat stress. It picks out 10 games at the two Texan venues which have a one-in-three chance of exceeding 28 degrees WBGT, including England v Croatia in Dallas on June 17.

The report’s authors listed several reasons why fans are perhaps the most vulnerable people at the tournament this summer, as they are likely to be less fit, older and less aware of the dangers of extreme heat than the players. They may also also be dehydrated from drinking alcohol or have pre-existing medical conditions that put them at risk.

The report also points out that the stadiums in Kansas City, Miami and New York/New Jersey are potentially “high risk” for both players and fans, as they do not have roofs or cooling systems.

When asked what impact these conditions are likely to have on the players, Mullington noted that, unlike athletes in marathons or triathlons, footballers can “self-pace” and just slow down by sitting back and letting their opponents’ defenders keep the ball.

In a long statement issued to The Athletic, FIFA defended its “tiered heat mitigation model” and said it was “committed to protecting the health and safety of players, referees, fans, volunteers and staff”.

It also explained that “when forecasts indicate elevated temperatures”, fans will be allowed to bring “one factory-sealed water bottle” into the stadium, where there will be “additional cooling capacity”, including shaded areas, misting systems, cooling buses and expanded water stations. Staff and volunteers will be given additional breaks, with precautions taken to deal with any potential heat illness.

In terms of player welfare, FIFA pointed out that as well as the introduction of the mandatory water breaks, it has recently increased the number of substitutes each team can use to five, with an additional substitute in extra time, and said there will be “climate-controlled benches” for the coaches and substitutes at all outdoor matches.

As noted by FIFPro, FIFA said it had also limited the number of outdoor matches during the hottest parts of the day and tried to give matches in “warmer windows” to stadiums with roofs.

Other measures include training sessions for each participating nation’s team doctors on heat mitigation, strengthened risk management and evacuation procedures, and close cooperation with the meteorological authorities in Canada, Mexico and the United States.

“Through close collaboration with host governments, medical experts and emergency authorities, FIFA remains committed to delivering a safe, resilient and memorable tournament experience for everyone involved,” it added.
